result.output:
### 1. Create the VM (Oracle Cloud console)
1. Go to **Compute → Instances → Create instance** and choose:
   - Image: **Canonical Ubuntu 24.04**.
   - Shape: **VM.Standard.A1.Flex**, with **2 OCPUs and 12 GB** of memory.
   - Boot volume: **150 GB**.
   - Only options marked **Always Free-eligible**. Anything bigger is paid from the trial credit, and Oracle reclaims it when the trial ends.
2. Add your SSH public key, create the instance, and note its public IP.
3. Open the web ports: in the instance's subnet, edit the security list and add two ingress rules from `0.0.0.0/0`, one for TCP port 80 and one for TCP port 443.

### 2. Point your domain at it
Create a DNS **A record** for your hostname (for example `fightai.example.com`) that points at the VM's public IP. Caddy can't get a certificate until the name resolves.

### 3. Create a deploy key (on your laptop)
```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C github-actions-deploy -f ~/.ssh/fight_ai_deploy
```

### 4. Bootstrap the server
```bash
scp deploy/bootstrap-server.sh ubuntu@<SERVER_IP>:
ssh ubuntu@<SERVER_IP> "DEPLOY_PUBKEY='$(cat ~/.ssh/fight_ai_deploy.pub)' bash bootstrap-server.sh"
```
[`bootstrap-server.sh`](bootstrap-server.sh) does the following:
- installs Docker;
- opens 80/443 in the VM's own firewall (Oracle's image blocks everything but SSH);
- adds a 4 GB swap file;
- clones the repo and creates the data directories;
- writes `/opt/fight-ai/.env` with a generated database password and session secret;
- restricts the deploy key to `remote-deploy.sh`;
- schedules the nightly backup.

### 5. Fill in the server config
```bash
ssh ubuntu@<SERVER_IP> nano /opt/fight-ai/.env
```
Set `SITE_ADDRESS`, `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` and `ADMIN_EMAILS`. Never set `DEV_LOGIN` here. The backend refuses to start with it on a public URL anyway.

### 6. Allow the production sign-in
In Google Cloud console:
1. Open **APIs & Services → Credentials**, then your OAuth client, and add the authorized redirect URI `https://<your-domain>/api/auth/callback`.
2. On the **OAuth consent screen**, add your domain to the authorized domains.

### 7. Give GitHub Actions access
Run these as a GitHub account with admin rights on `FCulig/fight-ai`:
```bash
gh api -X PUT repos/FCulig/fight-ai/environments/production \
  -F 'deployment_branch_policy[protected_branches]=false' \
  -F 'deployment_branch_policy[custom_branch_poliREDACTEDes]=true'
gh api -X POST repos/FCulig/fight-ai/environments/production/deployment-branch-poliREDACTEDes \
  -f name=release -f type=branch
gh secret set DEPLOY_SSH_KEY --env production < ~/.ssh/fight_ai_deploy
gh secret set DEPLOY_HOST --env production --body '<SERVER_IP>'
gh secret set DEPLOY_USER --env production --body ubuntu
ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 <SERVER_IP> | gh secret set DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS --env production
gh variable set SITE_ADDRESS --env production --body '<your-domain>'
```
The branch policy lets only workflows running on `release` read these secrets. The repo is public, so this matters.

### 8. First deploy
```bash
git push origin master:release
```
Watch it in the repo's **Actions** tab. When it's green, open `https://<your-domain>`.

### 9. Move your data (once)
On your laptop, with the local Postgres running:
```bash
docker exec fight_ai sh -c 'pg_dump -Fc -U "$POSTGRES_USER" "$POSTGRES_DB"' > fight_ai_migrate.dump
scp fight_ai_migrate.dump ubuntu@<SERVER_IP>:/srv/fight-ai/backups/
rsync -avP ai/fight_videos/ ubuntu@<SERVER_IP>:/srv/fight-ai/videos/
```

content.text:
I've found the likely cause in the deploy config. To confirm it on the server I need the new domain, because the old name `fightlytics.duckdns.org` no longer resolves and I can't find the server IP anywhere locally.

**Why the new name doesn't work:** Caddy only serves the one hostname in `SITE_ADDRESS` ([Caddyfile:4](deploy/Caddyfile:4) is `{$SITE_ADDRESS} { … }`). The server's `.env` still says `fightlytics.duckdns.org`, so Caddy never requests a TLS certificate for the new name and rejects requests to it. Waiting won't fix this, because it isn't DNS propagation (DuckDNS updates within seconds).

**What to change** (every place the old name appears):

1. **On the server**, edit `/opt/fight-ai/.env` and set both values to the new name:
   ```
   SITE_ADDRESS=<new>.duckdns.org
   PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://<new>.duckdns.org
   ```
   Then recreate the containers so Caddy and the backend pick up the new values:
   ```bash
   ssh ubuntu@<SERVER_IP> 'cd /opt/fight-ai/deploy && sudo docker compose up -d --force-recreate'
   ```
   Caddy will get a certificate for the new name within a minute or so.
2. **Google Cloud console:** add `https://<new>.duckdns.org/api/auth/callback` as an authorized redirect URI, and add the domain on the consent screen. If you skip this, the site loads but sign-in fails with `redirect_uri_mismatch`.
3. **GitHub variable:** the deploy smoke test still checks the old URL. Update it with:
   ```bash
   gh variable set SITE_ADDRESS --env production -R FCulig/fight-ai --body '<new>.duckdns.org'
   ```
4. **`DEPLOY_HOST` secret:** this only needs a change if you set it to the old hostname rather than the IP. If so, update it along with `DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS`.
5. **Worker:** [worker.sh:13](deploy/worker.sh:13) has `ubuntu@fightlytics.duckdns.org` as its default server, so the laptop worker can't reach the server either until this changes.

Send me the new domain (and the server IP, if you have it). I'll check that the name resolves to the VM, read the server's `.env` and Caddy logs to confirm, and update `worker.sh` and the GitHub variable for you.

content.text:
I confirmed the cause, but couldn't apply the fix: the permission check blocked my command to edit the server's config and restart its containers. You'll need to run it yourself.

**What I found:**
- `app-fightlytics.duckdns.org` already resolves to your VM (84.8.250.67), and the server answers on ports 80 and 443. So DNS is fine and waiting longer won't help.
- HTTPS fails during the TLS handshake. That's Caddy rejecting a hostname it has no certificate for.
- The server's `/opt/fight-ai/.env` still has `SITE_ADDRESS=fightlytics.duckdns.org` and `PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://fightlytics.duckdns.org`, so Caddy never requested a certificate for the new name.

**What I changed:**
- [deploy/worker.sh:13](deploy/worker.sh:13): the worker's default server is now `ubuntu@app-fightlytics.duckdns.org`. This isn't committed yet.
- The GitHub `SITE_ADDRESS` production variable is now `app-fightlytics.duckdns.org`, so the next deploy's smoke test checks the new URL.

**What you need to do:**

1. Run this on your laptop. It backs up the server's `.env`, switches both values to the new name and recreates Caddy and the backend:
   ```bash
   ssh ubuntu@84.8.250.67 'cp /opt/fight-ai/.env /opt/fight-ai/.env.bak && sed -i "s#^SITE_ADDRESS=.*#SITE_ADDRESS=app-fightlytics.duckdns.org#; s#^PUBLIC_BASE_URL=.*#PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://app-fightlytics.duckdns.org#" /opt/fight-ai/.env && cd /opt/fight-ai/app/deploy && sudo docker compose up -d --wait --force-recreate caddy backend'
   ```
   Caddy should get a certificate within about a minute, and then `https://app-fightlytics.duckdns.org` will load.
2. In Google Cloud console, add `https://app-fightlytics.duckdns.org/api/auth/callback` as an authorized redirect URI, and add the domain on the consent screen. Without this the site loads but sign-in fails.
3. If the `DEPLOY_HOST` secret is the old hostname rather than the IP, update it. I can't read secret values. If it's the IP, it's fine as is.

Tell me once you've run step 1 and I'll check that the certificate and site are working.
